stem: The energy received by the Earth from the Sun in the form of short waves (radiation) is called:
solution: Insolation (a contraction of 'INcoming SOLar radiATION') is the solar energy received by the Earth from the Sun, in the form of short-wave radiation. The Sun is the ultimate source of energy for the Earth's atmosphere; the energy it radiates travels through space and reaches the Earth as insolation. Because the Sun is very hot, its radiation is in short wavelengths (short waves). Understanding the term insolation (incoming short-wave solar radiation) is a fundamental prelims point. Insolation is the incoming short-wave solar radiation received by the Earth.

stem: The Earth receives only a very tiny fraction (about one two-billionth) of the total energy radiated by the Sun, mainly because:
options: The Sun is not very hot
The Earth is a small target at a very great distance from the Sun
The atmosphere blocks most of it
solution: The Earth receives only about one two-billionth (a very tiny fraction) of the total energy radiated by the Sun in all directions. This is because the Sun radiates its energy in every direction into space, and the Earth — being a relatively small body located at a very great distance from the Sun (about 150 million km away) — intercepts only a minute portion of this outpouring of energy. Despite being so tiny a fraction, this insolation is more than enough to power the Earth's atmosphere, weather, and life. Understanding why the Earth gets only a tiny fraction of solar energy (small, distant target) is a prelims point. The Earth receives a tiny fraction of solar energy because it is a small, distant target.

stem: Solar radiation (insolation) is in the form of __________ waves, while the Earth radiates energy back in the form of __________ waves.
solution: Solar radiation (insolation) is in the form of short waves (short-wavelength radiation), because the Sun is very hot (a hotter body radiates in shorter wavelengths). The Earth, being much cooler than the Sun, radiates its energy back into space in the form of long waves (long-wavelength/infrared radiation) — this outgoing radiation is called terrestrial radiation. This difference is fundamental to the greenhouse effect: the atmosphere is fairly transparent to incoming short-wave solar radiation but absorbs much of the outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation (trapping heat). Understanding that insolation is short-wave and terrestrial radiation is long-wave is a key prelims point. Insolation is short-wave; terrestrial (outgoing Earth) radiation is long-wave.

stem: The amount of insolation received at a place depends most importantly on the:
options: Angle of the sun's rays (the angle of incidence) — the more slanting the rays, the less the insolation
solution: The amount of insolation received at a place depends most importantly on the angle of the Sun's rays — the angle of incidence at which the rays strike the surface. When the Sun's rays are more vertical (overhead), the energy is concentrated over a smaller area (and passes through less atmosphere), so insolation is greater; when the rays are more slanting/oblique (low in the sky), the same energy is spread over a larger area (and passes through more atmosphere, losing more energy), so insolation is less. This is why the equator (where rays are more vertical) receives more insolation than the poles (where rays are very slanting). (Other factors include the length of day, transparency of the atmosphere, and the Sun-Earth distance.) Understanding that the angle of the Sun's rays is the key control on insolation is a prelims point. Insolation depends most on the angle of the Sun's rays — vertical rays give more, slanting rays give less.

stem: The equatorial regions receive more insolation than the polar regions mainly because:
options: The equator is closer to the Sun
Near the equator the Sun's rays fall nearly vertically (concentrated over a small area), while near the poles they fall very obliquely (spread over a large area)
The equator is at a higher altitude
solution: The equatorial regions receive more insolation than the polar regions mainly because of the angle at which the Sun's rays strike: near the equator, the Sun is high in the sky and its rays fall nearly vertically (perpendicular), concentrating the energy over a small area (and passing through less atmosphere); near the poles, the Sun is always low in the sky and its rays strike very obliquely (slanting), spreading the same energy over a much larger area (and passing through more atmosphere, so more is absorbed/scattered/reflected on the way). Hence the tropics are hot and the poles are cold. (It is not because the equator is physically 'closer' to the Sun.) Understanding this angle-of-rays explanation for the equator-pole insolation difference is a key prelims point. The equator gets more insolation than the poles because its rays are more vertical (concentrated) rather than slanting.

stem: As solar radiation passes through the atmosphere, part of it is sent back to space directly by reflection from clouds and the surface. The proportion of insolation reflected back to space is called the Earth's:
solution: Albedo is the proportion (fraction, or percentage) of incoming solar radiation (insolation) that is reflected back to space — by clouds, by atmospheric particles, and by the Earth's surface — without being absorbed. The Earth's average albedo is about 30–35% (that is, roughly a third of the incoming insolation is reflected straight back to space). Different surfaces have different albedos: bright surfaces like fresh snow and ice, and clouds, have high albedo (reflect a lot), while dark surfaces like forests and oceans have low albedo (absorb more). Understanding the term albedo (the reflected fraction of insolation) is a prelims point. Albedo is the fraction of insolation reflected back to space.

stem: The heating of the atmosphere and the transfer of heat within it involves several processes. The transfer of heat by the actual physical movement (rising) of heated air (as warm air rises and cool air sinks) is called:
solution: Convection is the transfer of heat by the actual physical movement (mass movement) of a heated fluid (air or water). In the atmosphere, when air near the surface is heated, it becomes lighter (less dense) and rises, carrying heat upward, while cooler, denser air sinks to take its place — setting up vertical convection currents that transfer heat upward through the troposphere. Convection is a very important process in heating the troposphere and in producing clouds and precipitation. (Contrast: conduction transfers heat by contact; advection transfers heat by horizontal air movement; radiation transfers heat by waves without a medium.) Understanding convection (vertical heat transfer by moving air) is a prelims point. Convection is the transfer of heat by the vertical movement (rising) of heated air.

stem: The transfer of heat through matter by molecular contact, from a warmer to a cooler part (as when the surface heats the air layer in direct contact with it), is called:
solution: Conduction is the transfer of heat through matter by molecular activity/contact — from a warmer part (or body) to a cooler part (or body) that is in direct contact with it, without the matter itself moving from place to place. In the atmosphere, conduction operates where the air is in direct contact with the warm (or cold) ground: the layer of air touching the Earth's surface is heated (or cooled) by conduction from the surface. Conduction is important only for the lowest layers of the atmosphere (in contact with the surface), since air is a poor conductor of heat. Understanding conduction (heat transfer by contact) is a prelims point. Conduction is the transfer of heat by molecular contact between a warmer and a cooler body in contact.

stem: The horizontal transfer of heat by the movement of air (wind) from one place to another is called:
solution: Advection is the horizontal transfer of heat by the horizontal movement of air — that is, by winds carrying warm or cold air from one region to another. For example, warm winds blowing from the tropics toward higher latitudes carry (advect) heat poleward, and cold winds carry cold air. In some regions, advection is very important: for instance, the hot 'loo' winds of northern India in summer are an example of heat brought by advection. (Contrast: convection is vertical heat transfer by rising air; conduction is by contact.) Understanding advection (horizontal heat transfer by wind) is a prelims point. Advection is the horizontal transfer of heat by the movement of air (wind).

stem: The Earth, after absorbing insolation, radiates energy back into space as long-wave radiation. This outgoing radiation from the Earth is called:
solution: Terrestrial radiation is the outgoing radiation emitted by the Earth (its surface and atmosphere) back into space, after the Earth has absorbed the incoming solar radiation (insolation). Because the Earth is much cooler than the Sun, its terrestrial radiation is in the form of long waves (long-wavelength/infrared radiation). The atmosphere (especially its greenhouse gases and water vapour) absorbs much of this outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation, which warms the atmosphere — the mechanism of the greenhouse effect. Understanding terrestrial radiation (outgoing long-wave Earth radiation) is a prelims point. Terrestrial radiation is the outgoing long-wave radiation emitted by the Earth.

stem: The atmosphere is heated mainly:
options: Directly by the Sun's short-wave radiation from above
From below — by the long-wave terrestrial radiation emitted by the Earth's surface (which the surface first absorbs from the Sun)
It is not heated at all
solution: The atmosphere is heated mainly from below — that is, by the long-wave terrestrial radiation emitted by the Earth's surface, not directly by the Sun's rays from above. This is because the atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming short-wave solar radiation (insolation), which mostly passes through it and is absorbed by the Earth's surface; the surface, thus heated, then radiates the energy back as long-wave (terrestrial) radiation, which the atmosphere (its water vapour and CO2) readily absorbs. So the surface acts as the direct source of heat for the atmosphere, warming it from below — which is also why temperature decreases with height in the troposphere. Understanding that the atmosphere is heated from below (by terrestrial radiation) is a key prelims point. The atmosphere is heated mainly from below, by long-wave terrestrial radiation from the Earth's surface.

stem: Over the Earth as a whole and over the year, the amount of incoming solar radiation (insolation) is balanced by the outgoing terrestrial radiation. This balance is called the:
options: Heat budget (heat balance) of the Earth
solution: The heat budget (or heat balance) of the Earth is the balance, over the whole Earth and over the year, between the incoming solar radiation (insolation) that the Earth receives and the outgoing terrestrial radiation that it emits back to space. Because the Earth's average temperature remains fairly constant over time, the amount of heat received must equal the amount of heat lost — the two are in balance (the Earth neither continuously heats up nor cools down overall). This balance is the heat budget. (If, for example, of 100 units of incoming insolation, some are reflected — albedo — and the rest absorbed and eventually re-radiated, the incoming and outgoing must balance.) Understanding the concept of the Earth's heat budget/balance is a prelims point. The heat budget is the balance between incoming insolation and outgoing terrestrial radiation over the whole Earth.

stem: Although the Earth's overall heat budget is balanced, there is an imbalance by latitude: regions between roughly __________ have a surplus of heat, while the higher latitudes have a deficit.
solution: Although the Earth's total heat budget is balanced, this balance does not hold at every latitude. The lower latitudes — roughly between 40°N and 40°S (the tropics and subtropics) — receive more insolation than they lose by terrestrial radiation, so they have a surplus (net gain) of heat; the higher latitudes (poleward of about 40°) lose more heat than they receive, so they have a deficit (net loss). This latitudinal imbalance (surplus in the tropics, deficit at the poles) drives the transfer of heat from the equator toward the poles (by winds and ocean currents), which prevents the tropics from getting ever hotter and the poles from getting ever colder. Understanding this latitudinal heat surplus/deficit (surplus ~40°N–40°S) is a prelims point. Lower latitudes (about 40°N to 40°S) have a heat surplus; higher latitudes have a deficit.

stem: The latitudinal imbalance of heat (surplus in the tropics, deficit at the poles) is corrected by the transfer of heat from the equator toward the poles, carried out mainly by:
options: The rotation of the Earth alone
solution: The latitudinal imbalance of heat — the surplus in the tropics (lower latitudes) and the deficit toward the poles (higher latitudes) — is corrected by the poleward transfer of heat, carried out mainly by winds (the general atmospheric circulation) and ocean currents. Warm winds and warm ocean currents carry heat from the surplus tropical regions toward the deficit polar regions, while cold winds and currents return cooler air/water toward the tropics. This continuous redistribution of heat keeps the tropics from overheating and the poles from becoming ever colder, maintaining the overall balance. Understanding that winds and ocean currents transfer heat poleward is a prelims point. Winds and ocean currents transfer surplus heat from the tropics toward the poles.

stem: The temperature of the air, as measured near the Earth's surface, is called the:
solution: Air temperature is the temperature (degree of hotness or coldness) of the air, as measured (typically) near the Earth's surface (in the shade, in a standard instrument shelter, at about 1.2–2 m above the ground). Air temperature results from the heating of the atmosphere (mainly from below, by terrestrial radiation), and it varies with time (day/night, season) and place (latitude, altitude, etc.). It is measured with a thermometer and expressed in degrees Celsius (or Fahrenheit). Understanding the concept of air temperature is a prelims point. Air temperature is the temperature of the air measured near the Earth's surface.

stem: Which of the following is the MOST important factor controlling the temperature distribution over the Earth?
options: Latitude (which determines the angle of the Sun's rays and length of day)
solution: Latitude is the most important factor controlling the distribution of temperature over the Earth. This is because latitude determines the angle at which the Sun's rays strike (more vertical near the equator, more slanting toward the poles) and the length of daylight — both of which control the amount of insolation received. As a result, temperatures are generally highest near the equator (low latitudes) and decrease toward the poles (high latitudes). (Other factors that affect temperature include altitude, distance from the sea/continentality, ocean currents, winds, and cloud cover — but latitude is the primary control.) Understanding that latitude is the chief control of temperature distribution is a prelims point. Latitude is the most important factor controlling the distribution of temperature.

stem: Temperature generally __________ with increasing altitude (height above sea level), which is why hill stations and high mountains are cooler than the plains.
solution: Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude (height above sea level) — at the normal lapse rate of about 6.5°C per 1000 m in the troposphere. This is because the atmosphere is heated mainly from below (by the Earth's surface radiating heat), so the air is warmest near the surface and cooler higher up. This is why hill stations and high mountains (like Shimla or the Himalayas) are cooler than the low-lying plains at the same latitude, and why high peaks can have snow even in the tropics. Understanding that temperature decreases with altitude is a prelims point. Temperature decreases with increasing altitude.

stem: Places near the sea (coastal areas) have a more __________ (moderate/equable) climate than places in the interior of continents, because the sea warms and cools more slowly than land.
solution: Places near the sea (coastal areas) have a more moderate (equable) climate — with smaller differences between day and night, and between summer and winter temperatures — than places in the interior of continents, which have a more extreme (continental) climate. This is because the sea (water) warms up and cools down much more slowly than the land: the ocean moderates the temperature of nearby coastal areas (keeping them cooler in summer and warmer in winter), and sea breezes carry this moderating influence inland. Far from the sea, in continental interiors, the land heats and cools rapidly, giving hot summers and cold winters (large temperature range). This influence of the sea is called the 'maritime' effect (and its absence inland, 'continentality'). Understanding that nearness to the sea moderates temperature is a prelims point. Coastal areas have a moderate (equable) climate because the sea warms and cools slowly.

stem: The difference between the maximum and minimum temperature (for a day, or for a year) at a place is called the:
solution: The range of temperature at a place is the difference between the maximum (highest) and minimum (lowest) temperature over a given period. The 'diurnal (daily) range' is the difference between the day's maximum and minimum temperatures; the 'annual range' is the difference between the mean temperature of the warmest and the coldest month of the year. Continental interiors (far from the sea) have large temperature ranges (extreme climate), while coastal/maritime areas have small ranges (equable climate). Understanding the concept of temperature range is a prelims point. The range of temperature is the difference between the maximum and minimum temperatures.

stem: The lines drawn on a map joining places that have the same temperature are called:
solution: Isotherms are the lines drawn on a map joining (connecting) places that have the same temperature (at a given time, or on average). ('Iso' = equal, 'therm' = temperature/heat.) Isotherm maps are used to show the distribution of temperature over the Earth's surface. (Similarly: isobars join places of equal pressure; isohyets join places of equal rainfall; and contours join places of equal height/elevation.) Understanding isotherms (lines of equal temperature) is a prelims point. Isotherms are lines joining places of equal temperature.

stem: In general, isotherms tend to run roughly __________ (following the parallels of latitude), because temperature is controlled largely by latitude.
solution: In general, isotherms (lines of equal temperature) tend to run roughly east-west, more or less parallel to the parallels of latitude. This is because temperature is controlled largely by latitude (the angle of the Sun's rays), so places along the same latitude tend to have similar temperatures, and the temperature changes mainly as one moves north or south (from the equator toward the poles). However, isotherms are not perfectly straight or parallel to latitude — they bend and deviate due to other influences such as the distribution of land and sea, ocean currents, altitude, and winds. Understanding that isotherms broadly follow latitude (run east-west) is a prelims point. Isotherms generally run roughly east-west, parallel to the latitudes.

stem: Isotherms generally bend/deviate sharply where they cross from land to sea (or sea to land), showing the strong effect of __________ on temperature.
options: The differential heating of land and water (land and sea contrast)
solution: Isotherms generally bend or deviate sharply where they cross a coastline (from land to sea or sea to land), reflecting the strong effect of the differential heating of land and water (the contrast between land and sea) on temperature. Because land heats up and cools down faster than water, at the same latitude the land is warmer than the sea in summer and cooler in winter — so isotherms bend as they pass from a landmass to an ocean (poleward over the warmer surface and equatorward over the cooler one), especially in the northern hemisphere (which has more land). The relatively smoother, straighter isotherms over the southern hemisphere (more ocean) confirm this. Understanding that the land-sea contrast makes isotherms bend at coasts is a prelims point. Isotherms bend at coastlines because land and water heat and cool at different rates.

stem: Isotherms are generally more regular (straighter and more parallel to latitude) in the __________ hemisphere.
solution: Isotherms are generally more regular — straighter and more nearly parallel to the parallels of latitude — in the Southern Hemisphere. This is because the Southern Hemisphere is dominated by oceans (has much more water and much less land than the Northern Hemisphere): with a more uniform (mostly ocean) surface, temperature is controlled more purely by latitude, and there is less of the land-sea contrast that makes isotherms bend. In the Northern Hemisphere, the large landmasses (and their differential heating relative to the oceans) cause the isotherms to bend and become irregular. Understanding that isotherms are more regular in the (ocean-dominated) Southern Hemisphere is a prelims point. Isotherms are more regular in the Southern Hemisphere because it is dominated by oceans.

stem: The normal condition in the troposphere is that temperature decreases with height. When this is reversed — temperature INCREASES with height (a warmer layer over a colder layer) — the condition is called a temperature:
solution: A temperature inversion is a condition in which the normal decrease of temperature with height is reversed — that is, temperature increases with height, so that a layer of warmer air lies above a layer of colder air (the reverse of the usual arrangement). Temperature inversions commonly form on clear, calm, cold nights (especially in winter and in valleys), when the ground rapidly loses heat by radiation and cools the air just above it, so the air near the surface becomes colder than the air above. Inversions trap pollutants, smoke, and fog near the surface (leading to poor air quality and fog/smog). Understanding temperature inversion (temperature increasing with height) is a prelims point. A temperature inversion is a reversal in which temperature increases (rather than decreases) with height.

stem: Temperature inversions most commonly form:
options: On long, clear, calm, cold winter nights (when the ground rapidly loses heat by radiation)
solution: Temperature inversions most commonly form on long, clear, calm, cold winter nights. The ideal conditions are: clear skies (which allow the ground to radiate away its heat rapidly and cool quickly at night); calm air / no wind (so the cold air stays put near the surface and does not mix with the warmer air above); long nights (giving plenty of time for cooling); and dry, cold winter air. Under these conditions, the ground cools sharply by radiation, chilling the air in contact with it, so the surface air becomes colder than the air above — an inversion. Valleys are especially prone to inversions (cold, dense air drains down and collects on the valley floor). Understanding the conditions for inversion (clear, calm, cold, long nights) is a prelims point. Temperature inversions form on clear, calm, cold, long winter nights.

stem: During the daytime, the Sun's rays warm the ground, and the atmosphere is warmed indirectly. The maximum temperature of the day usually occurs:
options: In the early afternoon (a little after noon, around 2–3 pm), not exactly at noon
solution: The maximum (highest) temperature of the day usually occurs in the early afternoon — a little after noon, around 2 to 3 pm — not exactly at midday (12 pm). Although the Sun's insolation is strongest at noon (when the Sun is highest), the ground and air continue to gain more heat than they lose for some time after noon; the temperature keeps rising as long as incoming insolation exceeds outgoing radiation, reaching its peak in the early afternoon, after which it begins to fall. (Similarly, the minimum temperature occurs not at midnight but around dawn/sunrise, after the whole night of cooling.) This delay between peak insolation and peak temperature is a prelims-relevant point. The maximum daily temperature occurs in the early afternoon (around 2–3 pm), a little after noon.

stem: The insolation received at the surface varies during the day, being maximum around __________ and decreasing towards sunrise and sunset.
options: Noon (midday, when the Sun is highest)
solution: The insolation received at the surface is maximum around noon (midday), when the Sun is at its highest point in the sky and its rays strike most vertically (concentrated, and passing through the least atmosphere); it decreases towards sunrise and sunset, when the Sun is low in the sky and its rays are very slanting (spread out and passing through more atmosphere). This daily variation of insolation (peaking at noon) is the reason for the daily cycle of temperature (though the temperature peak lags a little after noon). Understanding that insolation peaks at noon is a prelims point. Insolation is maximum around noon, when the Sun is highest.

stem: Which of the following surfaces would have the HIGHEST albedo (reflect the most insolation)?
solution: Fresh, clean snow and ice have the highest albedo — they reflect the most incoming solar radiation (up to about 80–90% of the insolation falling on them) because they are bright and white. Dark surfaces such as forests, oceans, and dark soil have low albedo (they absorb most of the insolation and reflect little). This is why snow-covered regions stay cold (they reflect away much of the Sun's energy rather than absorbing it), and it creates a feedback: as ice melts, the darker surface exposed absorbs more heat, causing more warming and melting. Understanding that snow/ice has the highest albedo is a prelims point. Fresh snow and ice have the highest albedo, reflecting the most insolation.

stem: The heating of the layer of air in direct contact with the warm ground, followed by its rising, is an example of the atmosphere being heated by:
options: Conduction (from the ground) followed by convection (rising)
solution: The heating of the thin layer of air in direct contact with the warm ground is an example of conduction (heat passing from the warm surface to the touching air by molecular contact); and when this heated, lighter air then rises, carrying the heat upward, that is convection. So the near-surface air is warmed by conduction from the ground, and then the heat is spread upward through the troposphere by convection (rising air currents). Together with the absorption of long-wave terrestrial radiation, these processes (conduction and convection) heat the lower atmosphere from below. Understanding that near-surface air is heated by conduction and then convection is a prelims point. Air touching the warm ground is heated by conduction, then carries heat upward by convection.

stem: Of the insolation that reaches the top of the atmosphere, roughly what percentage is reflected back to space (the Earth's average albedo), on average?
solution: On average, about 34% (roughly one-third) of the insolation reaching the top of the atmosphere is reflected back to space — this is the Earth's average albedo. This reflection is done by the clouds, by the atmosphere (its gases and dust particles), and by the Earth's surface (bright surfaces like snow, ice, deserts). The remaining ~66% is absorbed (some by the atmosphere, most by the Earth's surface), and eventually re-radiated as long-wave terrestrial radiation, maintaining the heat balance. (Different textbooks cite slightly different figures around 30–35%.) Understanding the Earth's average albedo (~34%, about one-third) is a prelims point. About 34% (roughly one-third) of insolation is reflected back to space — the Earth's albedo.

stem: In continental interiors (far from the sea), summers are very hot and winters are very cold. This large seasonal temperature range is due to:
options: Continentality (distance from the moderating influence of the sea) — land heats and cools rapidly
solution: The large seasonal temperature range in continental interiors — very hot summers and very cold winters — is due to continentality: being far from the sea, and hence lacking the moderating (equable) influence of the ocean. Because land heats up and cools down rapidly (much faster than water), regions far inland experience great extremes — the land heats strongly in summer (hot) and cools strongly in winter (cold), giving a large annual temperature range (an 'extreme' or 'continental' climate). Coastal areas, by contrast, are moderated by the slowly-warming, slowly-cooling sea (an 'equable' or 'maritime' climate). Understanding continentality (distance from the sea → extreme temperatures) is a prelims point. Continental interiors have extreme temperatures because they lack the sea's moderating influence (continentality).

stem: Ocean currents affect the temperature of nearby coastal areas: a __________ ocean current raises the temperature of the coast it flows along.
solution: A warm ocean current raises (warms) the temperature of the coastal areas it flows along, while a cold ocean current lowers (cools) the temperature of the coasts along its path. For example, the warm North Atlantic Drift (Gulf Stream extension) keeps the coasts of north-western Europe warmer than their high latitude would suggest (ports stay ice-free in winter), while cold currents (like the Labrador or Peru current) chill the coasts they wash. So ocean currents are an important factor in the distribution of temperature. Understanding that warm currents warm coasts (and cold currents cool them) is a prelims point. A warm ocean current raises the temperature of the coast it flows along.

stem: The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave solar radiation but absorbs much of the outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation. This selective absorption, which keeps the Earth warm, is the basis of the:
solution: The greenhouse effect is based on the fact that the atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming short-wave solar radiation (letting most of it pass through to warm the surface) but readily absorbs much of the outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation emitted by the warmed Earth (trapping this heat instead of letting it all escape to space). The greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane, etc. — do this absorbing, re-radiating heat back toward the surface and keeping the lower atmosphere and Earth warmer than they would otherwise be (much as the glass of a greenhouse traps heat). This natural greenhouse effect makes the Earth warm enough for life; its enhancement by human-added greenhouse gases causes global warming. Understanding the greenhouse effect (atmosphere traps outgoing long-wave radiation) is a prelims point. The greenhouse effect: the atmosphere passes incoming short-wave radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave radiation, warming the Earth.

stem: The length of the day (duration of sunlight) affects insolation: places and seasons with __________ days receive more total insolation.
solution: The length of the day (the duration of daylight/sunshine) is an important factor affecting insolation: the longer the day (the more hours of sunlight), the more total insolation a place receives (because it is exposed to the Sun's radiation for a longer time). This is one reason summers (with long days) are warmer than winters (with short days), and it also affects the latitudinal distribution of insolation over the year. So both the angle of the Sun's rays and the length of the day together determine how much insolation a place gets. Understanding that longer days give more insolation is a prelims point. Longer days (more hours of sunlight) mean more total insolation.

stem: Which of the following processes does NOT require a material medium (can transfer energy through the vacuum of space)?
solution: Radiation is the process that does not require a material medium — it can transfer energy (heat/light) through the vacuum of empty space, in the form of electromagnetic waves. This is how the Sun's energy travels across the vacuum of space to reach the Earth (as insolation). In contrast, conduction requires matter in direct contact (molecular transfer), and convection and advection require the physical movement of a material fluid (air or water) — so all three of these need a medium and cannot operate through a vacuum. Understanding that radiation alone needs no medium is a prelims point. Radiation, unlike conduction, convection, and advection, needs no material medium and can pass through the vacuum of space.

stem: Compared with equal areas of land, the oceans and seas heat up and cool down __________, giving them a moderating effect on nearby climates.
options: At the same rate as land
solution: Compared with land, the oceans and seas (water) heat up and cool down more slowly (they have a much greater capacity to store heat, and heat is mixed through a depth of water). Because water warms and cools slowly, the sea does not reach the extremes of temperature that land does — so it stays relatively cool in summer and relatively warm in winter, and it moderates the climate of nearby coastal areas (giving them an equable, maritime climate). Land, by contrast, heats and cools rapidly, giving extreme (continental) temperatures inland. This differential heating of land and water is a key control of temperature distribution. Understanding that water heats/cools more slowly than land is a prelims point. Oceans heat and cool more slowly than land, moderating nearby climates.

stem: The minimum temperature of the day is usually recorded:
options: Just before/around sunrise (early morning), after the whole night of cooling
solution: The minimum (lowest) temperature of the day is usually recorded just before, or around, sunrise (in the early morning) — not at midnight. This is because, through the night, there is no incoming insolation, and the ground and air continuously lose heat by radiation, cooling steadily all night long; the temperature keeps falling until the Sun rises and insolation begins again, so the coldest point is reached around dawn (just before/at sunrise). (Correspondingly, the maximum temperature is reached in the early afternoon, a little after noon.) Understanding that the daily minimum temperature occurs around sunrise is a prelims point. The minimum daily temperature is usually reached around sunrise, after the whole night's cooling.

stem: In a temperature inversion in a valley on a cold winter night, the coldest air is found:
options: At the bottom of the valley (cold, dense air drains down and collects there)
In the middle of the slope
solution: In a temperature inversion in a valley on a cold, calm winter night, the coldest air is found at the bottom of the valley. This is because, on a clear, calm night, the ground and the air in contact with it cool rapidly by radiation; the cold air, being denser (heavier), flows/drains downhill under gravity and collects (pools) on the valley floor, while warmer air sits above it on the slopes. This produces an inversion, with the coldest air at the valley bottom and warmer air up the slopes — which is why frost, fog, and cold are concentrated on valley floors (and why orchards and settlements in hill areas are often placed on the slopes rather than the valley bottom). Understanding valley inversions (coldest air at the valley floor) is a prelims point. In a valley inversion, the coldest, densest air drains down and collects at the valley bottom.

stem: The factors that control the temperature distribution over the Earth's surface include latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, and:
options: Prevailing winds and cloud cover (and the nature of the surface)
solution: The main factors that control the distribution of temperature over the Earth's surface are: latitude (the chief control — angle of the Sun's rays and length of day); altitude (temperature falls with height); distance from the sea / continentality (coasts equable, interiors extreme); ocean currents (warm currents warm coasts, cold currents cool them); prevailing winds (warm or cold winds carry their temperatures to the regions they blow over); cloud cover (clouds reduce daytime heating and reduce nighttime cooling, lowering the temperature range); and the nature of the land surface (albedo, vegetation, etc.). Together these factors explain the pattern of temperatures across the globe. Understanding the full set of temperature-controlling factors is a prelims point. Temperature distribution is controlled by latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, prevailing winds, and cloud cover.

stem: Cloudy nights tend to be __________ than clear nights, because clouds trap the outgoing terrestrial (long-wave) radiation and reduce the cooling of the surface.
solution: Cloudy nights tend to be warmer than clear nights. This is because clouds absorb and re-radiate the outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation emitted by the Earth's surface, trapping much of this heat and radiating part of it back down to the surface — acting like a 'blanket' that slows the loss of heat at night. On a clear night, by contrast, the surface radiates its heat freely and directly to space, cooling rapidly (which is why clear, calm nights are cold and prone to frost and inversions). So clouds reduce nighttime cooling (warmer nights) — just as they reduce daytime heating (cooler days) — thereby lowering the daily temperature range. Understanding why cloudy nights are warmer is a prelims point. Cloudy nights are warmer because clouds trap and re-radiate the outgoing terrestrial radiation, reducing surface cooling.

stem: The insolation received at the top of the atmosphere varies according to the Earth's distance from the Sun. The Earth's orbit being slightly elliptical, the Earth is nearest the Sun (perihelion) around __________.
solution: Because the Earth's orbit around the Sun is slightly elliptical (not a perfect circle), the Earth's distance from the Sun varies through the year. The Earth is nearest to the Sun (a position called perihelion) around 3rd January, and farthest from the Sun (aphelion) around 4th July. As a result, the Earth receives slightly more insolation in early January (perihelion) and slightly less in early July (aphelion). (Note: this variation in distance is a minor effect; it is NOT the cause of the seasons — the seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis. Indeed, the Northern Hemisphere has winter in January, when the Earth is closest to the Sun.) Understanding perihelion (~3rd Jan) and aphelion (~4th July) is a prelims point. The Earth is nearest the Sun (perihelion) around 3rd January and farthest (aphelion) around 4th July.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes the direction of net heat transfer that keeps the Earth's climate in balance?
options: From the poles toward the equator
From the surplus (low) latitudes toward the deficit (high) latitudes — i.e., from the equator toward the poles
There is no net heat transfer
solution: The net transfer of heat that keeps the Earth's climate in balance is directed from the surplus (low) latitudes toward the deficit (high) latitudes — that is, from the equator/tropics toward the poles. Because the tropics (roughly 40°N–40°S) receive more heat than they lose (surplus) and the higher latitudes lose more than they receive (deficit), heat is continuously carried poleward — by winds (atmospheric circulation) and ocean currents — from the hot surplus regions to the cold deficit regions. This poleward heat transfer prevents the tropics from overheating and the poles from getting ever colder, maintaining the balance. Understanding the equator-to-pole direction of net heat transfer is a prelims point. Net heat is transferred from the surplus tropics toward the deficit poles (equator to poles).

stem: Assertion (A): The atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial radiation than by direct solar radiation. Reason (R): The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave solar radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the atmosphere is heated more by terrestrial radiation (the long-wave radiation from the Earth's surface) than by direct solar radiation. And the reason for this (R) is that the atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming short-wave solar radiation — most of which passes straight through the atmosphere to be absorbed by the surface — but it readily absorbs the outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation emitted by the warmed surface. Because the atmosphere absorbs the long-wave (terrestrial) radiation but not the short-wave (solar) radiation, it is heated mainly from below by terrestrial radiation — so R correctly explains A. Understanding this cause-effect (why the atmosphere is heated from below) is a prelims point. The atmosphere is heated mainly by terrestrial radiation because it absorbs long-wave but not short-wave radiation.

stem: The unit commonly used to measure temperature in most of the world (and in science) is the degree:
solution: The degree Celsius (°C), also called Centigrade, is the unit most commonly used to measure temperature in most of the world (and in most scientific and geographical work), on a scale where water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C (at standard pressure). (The Fahrenheit scale, °F, where water freezes at 32° and boils at 212°, is used mainly in the United States; the Kelvin scale, K, is the SI 'absolute' scale used in physics.) In Indian geography and daily use, temperature is expressed in degrees Celsius. Understanding that Celsius is the common unit of temperature is a basic prelims point. Temperature is commonly measured in degrees Celsius (°C).

stem: The amount of solar energy received on a unit area at the top of the atmosphere, when the Earth is at its mean distance from the Sun, is a nearly constant value called the:
solution: The solar constant is the (nearly constant) amount of solar energy received per unit area, per unit time, on a surface held perpendicular to the Sun's rays at the top of the atmosphere, when the Earth is at its mean (average) distance from the Sun. Its value is about 1.94 calories per square centimetre per minute (roughly 1367 watts per square metre). It is called a 'constant' because it varies only slightly. The solar constant represents the maximum insolation available at the top of the atmosphere; the amount actually reaching any point on the surface is less, and varies with the angle of the rays, atmospheric conditions, etc. Understanding the solar constant is a prelims point. The solar constant is the nearly-fixed amount of solar energy received per unit area at the top of the atmosphere at the Earth's mean distance.

stem: The daily (diurnal) range of temperature is generally GREATER in deserts than in coastal areas because:
options: In deserts the clear, dry, cloudless skies allow strong heating by day and rapid cooling by night (and there is no moderating sea)
solution: The daily (diurnal) range of temperature — the difference between the day's maximum and minimum — is generally much greater in deserts than in coastal areas. In deserts, the skies are usually clear, dry, and cloudless: by day, the strong insolation (with no clouds to block it) heats the sandy surface intensely (very hot days); by night, with no clouds and little water vapour to trap the outgoing radiation, the surface radiates its heat rapidly to space and cools sharply (cold nights). There is also no nearby sea to moderate the temperature. Hence deserts have very hot days and cold nights (a large diurnal range). Coastal areas, moderated by the sea and often cloudier/more humid, have a small diurnal range. Understanding why deserts have a large diurnal temperature range is a prelims point. Deserts have a large daily temperature range because clear, dry skies cause strong daytime heating and rapid nighttime cooling.

stem: The seasons of the year (summer, winter, etc.) are caused mainly by:
options: The changing distance of the Earth from the Sun
The tilt (inclination) of the Earth's axis and its revolution around the Sun (which change the angle of the Sun's rays and the length of day through the year)
The rotation of the Earth on its axis
solution: The seasons are caused mainly by the tilt (inclination) of the Earth's axis (about 23.5° to the vertical) combined with the Earth's revolution (orbit) around the Sun. Because the axis is tilted and keeps pointing the same way as the Earth goes round the Sun, different parts of the Earth are angled toward or away from the Sun at different times of year — so the angle of the Sun's rays and the length of daylight change through the year, giving the seasons. When a hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, it has summer (high sun, long days); when tilted away, it has winter (low sun, short days). (The seasons are NOT caused by the Earth's changing distance from the Sun — indeed the Earth is closest to the Sun in January, when the Northern Hemisphere has winter.) Understanding that the axial tilt (not distance) causes the seasons is a key prelims point. The seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis together with its revolution around the Sun.

stem: A cold ocean current flowing along a coast will __________ the temperature of that coastal region.
solution: A cold ocean current flowing along a coast will lower (reduce) the temperature of that coastal region, because the cold water chills the air above it, and this cooler air affects the adjacent land. For example, the cold Peru (Humboldt) Current cools the coast of Peru/Chile, and the cold Benguela Current cools the coast of south-western Africa — both contributing to cool, and often foggy and dry (desert), coasts. (Conversely, a warm current raises the temperature of the coasts it washes.) So ocean currents are an important control on coastal temperatures. Understanding that a cold current lowers coastal temperature is a prelims point. A cold ocean current lowers the temperature of the coast it flows along.

stem: Which instrument shelter/screen is used to house the thermometers so that air temperature is measured correctly (in the shade, protected from direct sunlight and rain)?
solution: The Stevenson Screen (thermometer screen) is the standard louvred wooden box/shelter used to house the thermometers (and other instruments) so that air temperature is measured correctly. It is painted white (to reflect sunlight), has louvred (slatted) sides to allow free air circulation while keeping out direct sunlight and rain, and is mounted at a standard height (about 1.2–1.25 m) above a grassy surface. This ensures the thermometer measures the true temperature of the freely-circulating air in the shade, not the effect of direct sunlight, rain, or heat radiated from the ground. (Other instruments: a barometer measures pressure, a rain gauge measures rainfall, an anemometer measures wind speed.) Understanding the Stevenson Screen (shelter for measuring air temperature) is a prelims point. The Stevenson Screen is the louvred shelter that houses thermometers for correct air-temperature measurement.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature' is that:
options: The Sun has no effect on the Earth

The Sun's energy (insolation), unequally received over the Earth (mainly because of the angle of the rays/latitude), heats the atmosphere from below and is redistributed so that the Earth maintains an overall heat balance, and temperature is distributed according to factors like latitude, altitude, and distance from the sea
Temperature is the same everywhere on Earth
The atmosphere is heated directly by the Sun from above
solution: The chapter conveys that the Sun is the ultimate source of energy for the Earth, supplying insolation (incoming short-wave solar radiation), which is received unequally over the Earth's surface — greatest at the equator (where the Sun's rays are near-vertical) and least at the poles (where they are very slanting), mainly because of the angle of the Sun's rays (a function of latitude) and the length of day. This insolation heats the Earth's surface, which in turn heats the atmosphere from below (by terrestrial long-wave radiation, conduction, and convection); and although some latitudes have a heat surplus (the tropics) and others a deficit (the poles), the transfer of heat by winds and ocean currents keeps the Earth in an overall heat balance (heat budget). The resulting distribution of temperature over the Earth is controlled by factors such as latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, prevailing winds, and cloud cover — shown on maps by isotherms. Understanding how solar radiation is received and unequally distributed, how the atmosphere is heated and the heat balanced, and what controls temperature is the central concern of this chapter, and it underlies the study of winds, pressure, and climate. The Sun's unequally-received energy heats the atmosphere from below, is balanced across latitudes, and gives a temperature distribution governed by latitude, altitude, and nearness to the sea.
